name: Iron
summary: An essential mineral needed to make hemoglobin, taken to prevent or treat iron deficiency and the anemia and fatigue it can cause.
what_it_is: Iron is an essential part of hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen, and of myoglobin, which supplies oxygen to muscles. Food contains heme iron, from meat, seafood and poultry, and nonheme iron, the only form in plants and fortified foods. Deficiency develops in stages, from depleted stores to iron-poor red blood cell production and finally iron deficiency anemia.

evidence.why: Dozens of randomized trials show iron supplements raise hemoglobin and iron stores and reduce anemia, and oral iron is first-line treatment for iron deficiency.

status_us.label: Dietary supplement (child-poisoning warning)
status_us.note: Sold as a dietary supplement. FDA requires iron-containing products to warn that accidental overdose is a leading cause of fatal poisoning in children under 6.

benefits.claim: Reduces anemia and iron deficiency and raises hemoglobin in menstruating women (67 trials, 8,506 women)
Appears to reduce fatigue and improve exercise performance in menstruating women
Lowers the risk of iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy, though US groups differ on routine supplementation
Oral iron is first-line treatment for iron deficiency with or without anemia that is not severe; IV iron is preferred when pills fail, aren't tolerated or aren't absorbed

risks.risk: Constipation, diarrhea, nausea, indigestion and metallic taste; in trials of menstruating women, bowel side effects were about twice as common as without iron
Accidental overdose can be fatal in young children; it caused about a third of US child poisoning deaths between 1983 and 1991
Iron overload in people with hemochromatosis, which untreated can lead to liver cirrhosis and heart disease
In anemia of chronic disease, supplementation is controversial because it may raise infection and cardiovascular risk

avoid_if: Anemia of chronic disease or inflammation (clinician first)
Unexplained iron deficiency, which can come from blood loss in the gut or from colon cancer (get evaluated first)
interactions: Levodopa: iron may reduce its absorption and effectiveness
Levothyroxine: iron can reduce its effectiveness
Proton pump inhibitors: reduce iron absorption and may blunt the response to iron supplements
Calcium may reduce iron absorption, and iron supplements can lower zinc absorption

before: Transferrin saturation or full iron studies if inflammation may make ferritin misleading
during: Complete blood count and ferritin to check the response
labs.why: Ferritin reflects iron stores and is the most efficient test for diagnosing iron deficiency, but inflammation raises it, and it reads misleadingly high soon after IV iron.

studies.title: Daily iron supplementation for improving anaemia, iron status and health in menstruating women
studies.finding: Daily iron reduced anemia and iron deficiency, raised hemoglobin and iron stores, improved exercise performance and appeared to reduce fatigue, with about twice the rate of bowel side effects.

studies.title: Diagnosis and management of iron deficiency in females
studies.people: Females with iron deficiency (review of guidelines and studies)
studies.finding: Recommends diagnosing with ferritin, adding full iron studies when inflammation is present, starting with oral iron, and using IV iron when oral iron fails, is not tolerated, is not absorbed or anemia is severe.

ask_your_clinician: Do my ferritin and hemoglobin results show that I need iron, and what is causing my deficiency?
Does iron interact with my thyroid, Parkinson's or acid-reducing medicines?
If iron pills upset my stomach or don't work, is IV iron an option for me?

sources.title: Iron supplementation taken daily for improving health in menstruating women
Diagnosis and management of iron deficiency in females

notes_for_editor: A 2012 CMAJ randomized trial of iron for fatigue in non-anemic women with low ferritin could not be opened, so the fatigue claim rests on the 2016 Cochrane review. ODS reports that ACOG recommends iron in pregnancy while USPSTF found the evidence insufficient for routine supplementation. The ODS URL contains encoded spaces exactly as returned by search; the clean URL was not reachable. The CMAJ review's title is taken from the search listing because the text read did not show it.
